ukmt-pink-2026-01.title: Estimate each one
ukmt-pink-2026-01.body:
B, D and E are all at least 200 (B is 202.6, D is 196, E is 520). C is $20+26=46$. A is $202\div6=33\tfrac13$, which is smaller than 46.

**Answer: (A) $202\div6$**

ukmt-pink-2026-02.title: Cut into four small triangles
ukmt-pink-2026-02.body:
Join the midpoints of the sides of the equilateral triangle to cut it into four congruent equilateral triangles. The line through the midpoint of $RS$ parallel to $PQ$ is one of these cutting lines, and the shaded region consists of one and a half of the four small triangles. So the shaded fraction is $\tfrac{1.5}{4}=\tfrac38$.

**Answer: (D) $\tfrac38$**

ukmt-pink-2026-03.title: Divisible by 2 and 3
ukmt-pink-2026-03.body:
A number is divisible by 6 if it is divisible by 2 and by 3. So $a$ is even. The digit sum is $1+9+3+3+9+1+a=26+a$, which must be a multiple of 3, so $a=1,4$ or $7$. The only even one is 4.

**Answer: (C) 4**

ukmt-pink-2026-04.title: Evaluate each bracket
ukmt-pink-2026-04.body:
Each bracket equals $-1$. There are $2026\div2=1013$ brackets. The first bracket is $-1$; each of the other 1012 brackets is subtracted, and subtracting $-1$ adds 1. So the value is $-1+1012=1011$.

**Answer: (C) 1011**

ukmt-pink-2026-05.title: Parity first
ukmt-pink-2026-05.body:
Number the boxes 1 to 7 from the left. Adjacent numbers sum to an odd number, so odd and even numbers alternate. Box 2 holds the even number 2, so boxes 2, 4, 6 are even and boxes 1, 3, 5, 7 are odd. The evens are 2, 4, 6, so boxes 4 and 6 hold 4 and 6 in some order. The odds are 1, 3, 5, 7 with 5 in box 7, so boxes 1, 3, 5 hold 1, 3, 7.

Boxes 1, 2, 3 sum to $2+$ (two of 1, 3, 7): $1+3+2=6$ and $3+7+2=12$ are multiples of 3, but $1+7+2=10$ is not. So boxes 1 and 3 hold 1 and 7, and box 5 holds 3.

Boxes 5, 6, 7 are $3,\ ?,\ 5$: with 4 in the middle the sum is 12, a multiple of 3, so box 6 holds 6 and box 4 holds 4 (and then $1,2,7,4,3,6,5$ or $7,2,1,4,3,6,5$ both work).

The shaded boxes are 4 and 5, containing $4+3=7$.

**Answer: (B) 7**

ukmt-pink-2026-06.title: Smallest possible counts
ukmt-pink-2026-06.body:
Let there be $n$ dogs. The counts of sheep, goats, pigs and chickens are at least $n+1$, $n+2$, $n+3$, $n+4$ respectively, and the chickens number $2n$. So $2n\ge n+4$, giving $n\ge4$. The total is as small as possible when $n=4$ and each count is as small as possible: $4,5,6,7,8$ (chickens $8=2\times4$). The total is $4+5+6+7+8=30$.

**Answer: (B) 30**

ukmt-pink-2026-07.title: Find Isobel
ukmt-pink-2026-07.body:
Gabriel and Jesseca have at most $13+14=27$ bites, so Isobel has at most $9$. If Isobel had 7, the pair would have 21, but no two of 9, 10, 13, 14 sum to 21. So Isobel has 9, and Gabriel and Jesseca have 13 and 14 in some order. Kyle and Henry have 7 and 10 in some order.

If Kyle had 10 and Henry 7, Jesseca would have $2\times7-10=4$, impossible. So Kyle has 7, Henry has 10 and Jesseca has $2\times10-7=13$.

**Answer: (D) 13**

ukmt-pink-2026-08.title: Neighbours of 2
ukmt-pink-2026-08.body:
The six primes are 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13. Adding 2 to 3, 5 or 11 gives a prime (5, 7, 13), but $2+7=9$ and $2+13=15$ are not prime. So the two neighbours of the 2 are 7 and 13, in either order (2 ways).

Any other two of the six primes are both odd, so their sum is even and greater than 2, hence not prime: no further restrictions. The other three primes can be placed in $3!=6$ ways. In total $2\times6=12$.

**Answer: (C) 12**

ukmt-pink-2026-09.title: Which regular polygons fit?
ukmt-pink-2026-09.body:
A regular $k$-gon with vertices among the 15 points needs $k$ to divide 15, so $k=3$, $5$ or $15$. A triangle uses every fifth point: there are 5 different triangles (one for each starting position $0,1,2,3,4$). A pentagon uses every third point: 3 different pentagons. There is 1 regular 15-gon. The total is $5+3+1=9$.

**Answer: (C) 9**

ukmt-pink-2026-10.title: Total turning
ukmt-pink-2026-10.body:
Walk once round the outline. The marked angles are ten interior angles of size $\alpha$, so at each of these corners you turn through $180^\circ-\alpha$. Because the outline crosses itself, going round the shape once makes two complete turns, so the total turning is $2\times360^\circ=720^\circ$. Hence $10(180^\circ-\alpha)=720^\circ$, so $180^\circ-\alpha=72^\circ$ and $\alpha=108^\circ$.

**Answer: (C) $108^\circ$**

ukmt-pink-2026-11.title: Count with corrections
ukmt-pink-2026-11.body:
The cube is $3\times3\times3$, so each tunnel passes through 3 small cubes. Six tunnels pass through at most $6\times3=18$ small cube-visits, which would leave $27-18=9$ undrilled cubes if there were no overlaps. But some cubes are drilled more than once. The centre cube is drilled by three tunnels, so it is counted twice too often. On the bottom layer, one small cube is drilled by two tunnels (from the left and from the right), counted once too often. So the number of drilled cubes is $18-2-1=15$ and the number of undrilled cubes is $27-15=12$.

**Answer: (B) 12**

ukmt-pink-2026-12.title: Who can be lying?
ukmt-pink-2026-12.body:
Exactly one pupil did not finish. If Qusay were lying, he would have finished, so someone else would not have, and that person would have to be lying too, contradicting that only one pupil lied. So Qusay is truthful and did not finish. Then the other four finished in positions 1 to 4.

Sara must be truthful: otherwise nobody could be fourth. Then Rathursan (who finished and was not fourth) is also truthful. If Priya were lying, she would be first or fourth, forcing Tanisha or Sara to be lying too. So Priya is truthful, and the liar must be Tanisha. The order is Rathursan, Tanisha, Priya, Sara or Rathursan, Priya, Tanisha, Sara.

**Answer: (E) Tanisha**

ukmt-pink-2026-13.title: Two repeating patterns
ukmt-pink-2026-13.body:
Both wheels leave a mark each time the wet part of the tyre touches the ground, so each wheel produces a regular pattern of marks, with a period equal to its circumference (small wheel: shorter period; large wheel: longer period). The track must therefore be made of two overlapping regular patterns.

Take the puddle as the zeroth mark. The first mark after the puddle must come from the small wheel, and this gives its period (the gaps between its marks). Options A and D would need the small wheel to have made marks where there are none, so they are ruled out. Now take the first mark not made by the small wheel: it is the first mark of the large wheel, which gives its period. In option E all marks are accounted for by these two regular patterns (for example with the puddle at 0 the small wheel marks fall at $3,6,9,\dots$ and the large wheel at $7,14,21$ in units of the dash length). In every other option some mark is left over.

**Answer: (E)**

ukmt-pink-2026-14.title: Compare with triangle PNQ
ukmt-pink-2026-14.body:
The shaded region is triangle $PNO$. Since $O$ is the centre of rectangle $MQRN$, $O$ is the midpoint of the diagonal $NQ$. Triangles $PNO$ and $PNQ$ share the side $PN$, and the distance from $O$ to the line $PN$ is half the distance from $Q$ to it, so $\text{area}(PNO)=\tfrac12\text{area}(PNQ)$.

Triangle $PNQ$ has base $PQ$ and the same height as the rectangle (since $N$ is on the opposite side), so its area is half of the rectangle. So the shaded fraction is $\tfrac12\times\tfrac12=\tfrac14$.

**Answer: (A) $\tfrac14$**

ukmt-pink-2026-15.title: Add the three line sums
ukmt-pink-2026-15.body:
Let $S$ be the common line sum. There are three lines (the vertical line of 5 boxes and two diagonal lines of 4 boxes). The three shaded boxes are the ones lying on two lines each (where the diagonals meet each other or the vertical line); every other box lies on exactly one line. Let the shaded boxes contain $a$, $b$, $c$. Adding the three line sums gives $3S=(1+2+\dots+10)+a+b+c=55+a+b+c$.

To maximise $S$ we maximise $a+b+c$ subject to $55+a+b+c$ being a multiple of 3. The largest sum $10+9+8=27$ gives $82$, which is not a multiple of 3. The next, $10+9+7=26$, gives $81$, so $S=27$. This can be achieved, as the filling in the official solution shows, so the three shaded numbers sum to 26.

**Answer: (D) 26**

ukmt-pink-2026-16.title: Each match adds 2 points
ukmt-pink-2026-16.body:
In a drawn match the two players get $1+1=2$ points. In a decisive match they get $3+(-1)=2$ points. So every match adds 2 to the total score, and there were $90\div2=45$ matches. With $n$ players there are $\tfrac{n(n-1)}2$ matches, so $n(n-1)=90=10\times9$ and $n=10$.

**Answer: (A) 10**

ukmt-pink-2026-17.title: Factorise
ukmt-pink-2026-17.body:
$a^b-ab=a(a^{b-1}-b)=2026=2\times1013$ with 1013 prime. So $a\in\{1,2,1013,2026\}$. The values $a=1013$ and $a=2026$ would need $a^{b-1}-b$ to equal 2 or 1, impossible for such large $a$ (for $b=1$ the left side is $1-1=0$, and for $b\ge2$ it is far too large). For $a=1$: $1-b=2026$ gives a negative $b$. For $a=2$: $2^{b-1}-b=1013$. Since $2^{10}=1024$, try $b=11$: $2^{10}-11=1013$ ✓. So $a=2$, $b=11$ and $a+b=13$.

**Answer: (B) 13**

ukmt-pink-2026-18.title: Express radii using distances
ukmt-pink-2026-18.body:
Let the $i$th small circle have radius $r_i$ and let its centre be at distance $d_i$ from the centre of the large circle. Since it touches the large circle (internally), $d_i+r_i=10$, so $r_i=10-d_i$.

Each side of the shaded polygon joins two neighbouring small-circle centres that touch each other, so its length is $r_i+r_{i+1}$. Going round the polygon, each radius is used twice, so the perimeter is $2(r_1+\dots+r_9)=2\big(90-(d_1+\dots+d_9)\big)=2(90-d)=180-2d$.

**Answer: (D) $180-2d$**

ukmt-pink-2026-19.title: Compare water and air
ukmt-pink-2026-19.body:
Upright, the water is a cylinder 24 cm high. Upside down, the total height of the cylinder part is 42 cm and the water has height 30 cm, so the air part, which is also a cylinder, is $42-30=12$ cm high. The water volume and the air volume are the volumes of cylinders of the same cross-section, with heights 24 cm and 12 cm, so water : air $=2:1$. The water is $\tfrac23$ of the capacity: $\tfrac23\times4.5=3.0$ litres.

**Answer: (E) 3.0 litres**

ukmt-pink-2026-20.title: Compare areas
ukmt-pink-2026-20.body:
Let $AB=x$ and let each hexagon have height $2h$. Cut everything by the horizontal line through the centres.

The part of the left hexagon not in the right hexagon is made of two parallelograms (one above and one below the middle line), each with horizontal side $x$ and height $h$, so the left-only region has area $2xh$. By symmetry the right-only region has the same area.

The overlap is made of two congruent trapezia, each of height $h$ with parallel sides of length $120-x$ (on the middle line: the width of a hexagon is 120) and $60-x$ (at the top edge). Its area is $2\cdot\tfrac{(120-x)+(60-x)}{2}h=(180-2x)h$.

The three regions have equal area, so $2xh=(180-2x)h$, giving $x=45$.

**Answer: (D) 45**

ukmt-pink-2026-21.title: Fibonacci growth
ukmt-pink-2026-21.body:
Order the lengths $a_1<a_2<\dots<a_8$. Three sticks cannot form a triangle if the longest is at least the sum of the other two, so we need $a_i\ge a_{i-1}+a_{i-2}$ for all $i\ge3$ (checking consecutive triples is enough, since any triple $x<y<z$ has $z\ge a_{j-1}+a_{j-2}\ge x+y$).

To keep the longest as short as possible, start with $1,2$ and take equality each time: $1,2,3,5,8,13,21,34$. Any other choice makes the terms at least as large, so the shortest possible longest stick is 34.

**Answer: (E) 34**

ukmt-pink-2026-22.title: Compare heights on a common base
ukmt-pink-2026-22.body:
Let $P$, $S$ be the bottom-left and bottom-right vertices of the hexagon and $V$ its right-hand vertex. One square is $PQRS$ (on side $PS$). The other square has side $SV$ and its vertex adjacent to $S$ inside the hexagon is $T$. Both squares have the same side, so $ST=SR$. The striped triangle has vertices $X,T,R$, where $X$ is the point where the side of the second square through $T$ meets the top side $QR$ of the first square; the shaded triangle is $TSR$.

The interior angle of the hexagon is $\angle PSV=120^\circ$ and $\angle TSV=90^\circ$, so $\angle PST=30^\circ$. Then $\angle TSR=\angle PSR-\angle PST=90^\circ-30^\circ=60^\circ$. Triangle $TSR$ has $ST=SR$ and a $60^\circ$ angle between them, so it is equilateral and $\angle RTS=\angle SRT=60^\circ$. Since $\angle STX=90^\circ$, $\angle XTR=30^\circ$. Also $\angle XRT=\angle QRS-\angle SRT=90^\circ-60^\circ=30^\circ$. So triangle $XTR$ is isosceles, and $X$ lies on the perpendicular bisector of $TR$, which also passes through $S$; let $Y$ be the midpoint of $TR$.

The two triangles have the common base $TR$ and heights $XY=TY\tan30^\circ=TY\cdot\tfrac{\sqrt3}3$ and $YS=TY\tan60^\circ=TY\sqrt3$. The ratio of the areas is $\tfrac{\sqrt3}{3}:\sqrt3=1:3$.

**Answer: (C) 1 : 3**

ukmt-pink-2026-23.title: Reflect the chords
ukmt-pink-2026-23.body:
Reflect each chord in the centre to get two more chords, one 3 cm and one 4 cm on the other side. The four chords cut the circle into 9 regions, and by symmetry the regions can be grouped by area: four corner regions of area $p$, two regions $q$ (above and below the central rectangle), two regions $r$ (left and right) and the central rectangle $s$, whose sides are $2\times3=6$ cm and $2\times4=8$ cm, so $s=48\ \text{cm}^2$.

In terms of these, $J=p$, $K=p+q$, $L=p+r$, $M=p+q+r+s$. Then $(J+M)-(K+L)=2p+q+r+s-(2p+q+r)=s=48$.

**Answer: (D) 48**

ukmt-pink-2026-24.title: Sum of odd numbers
ukmt-pink-2026-24.body:
Elijah takes $1,3,5,\dots$, and the sum of the first $n$ odd numbers is $n^2$. Since 407 is not a square, Elijah's last turn must have been the incomplete one (he took what was left). The largest square below 407 is $400=20^2$, so after 20 full turns Elijah has 400, and on his 21st turn (which would be for 41 toffees) he finds only 7 left. Mason took $2,4,\dots,40$ in his 20 turns, which is $400+20=420$ toffees. The total is $400+420+7=827$.

**Answer: (B) 827**

ukmt-pink-2026-25.title: Use the sum of all nine numbers
ukmt-pink-2026-25.body:
$a$ divides the sum of the other eight numbers exactly when it divides the sum of all nine. In the nine numbers each digit appears once as a hundreds digit, once as a tens digit and once as a units digit, so the sum is $45\times100+45\times10+45=45\times111=3^3\times5\times37$.

The three-digit divisors of this are $111, 135, 185, 333, 555, 999$. A number $a$ read off the circle has three distinct digits, which rules out 111, 333, 555, 999. Both 135 and 185 are possible (a computer search or construction confirms that each occurs). So there are 2 possible values.

**Answer: (B) 2**
